# feedback-sdk-widget

A framework-agnostic feedback button. Renders in Shadow DOM; themeable via CSS custom properties.

## Contract (frozen)

- Element: `<feedback-widget>`
- Attributes:
  - `endpoint` (required) -- the service HTTP base, e.g. `https://xxx.convex.site`
  - `token` (required) -- the project's public submit token (`fbk_...`)
  - `categories` (optional) -- comma-separated; default `idea,bug,other`
  - `page-context` (optional) -- default `location.pathname + location.search`
  - `label` (optional) -- button text; default `Feedback`
  - `submitter` (optional) -- identity string; omitted means anonymous
- Event: `feedback-submitted`, `CustomEvent<{ id: string }>`, bubbles + composed
- Theming: override `--fw-accent`, `--fw-surface`, `--fw-surface-strong`, `--fw-text`, `--fw-muted`, `--fw-border`, `--fw-radius`, `--fw-z`

## Usage

npm:

```js
import "feedback-sdk-widget";
// then place <feedback-widget endpoint="..." token="fbk_..."></feedback-widget>
```

script tag (self-mounts a floating button from data-attrs):

```html
<script src="https://.../feedback-widget.iife.js"
        data-endpoint="https://xxx.convex.site"
        data-token="fbk_..."></script>
```

Note: when serving the script from a public CDN, add Subresource Integrity
(`integrity="sha384-..." crossorigin="anonymous"`) using the hash of the built
file.

## Build outputs

- `dist/feedback-widget.js` -- ESM, registers the element on import
- `dist/feedback-widget.iife.js` -- self-mounting script-tag bundle

# feedback-sdk

A feedback button whose inbox is an agent work queue.

Drop a small widget into any app. Users (or you, while dogfooding) submit
feedback from inside the product. It lands in an isolated per-project store that
a coding agent reads and acts on -- so the loop is "hit a bug, type it in the
app, keep going," instead of stopping to re-explain it in a terminal.

Think Sentry, except the triager on the other end is your agent, not a dashboard.

## Status

Early, but usable from anywhere. The widget is published on npm as
[`feedback-sdk-widget`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/feedback-sdk-widget), and
the service runs either as a **local** Convex deployment (offline dev) or a
**cloud** deployment (a public URL any app or agent can reach). Multi-tenant
accounts, a provisioning CLI, and an MCP server are still ahead -- see Roadmap.

## What's here

```
convex/            the service: schema, projects, feedback, HTTP endpoints (two-key auth, CORS)
packages/client/   submitFeedback() -- the tiny POST the widget makes
packages/widget/   <feedback-widget> framework-agnostic web component (Shadow DOM, themeable)
examples/demo.html a standalone page to try the widget with no app
docs/TESTING.md    step-by-step: run it and test it yourself
docs/design/       the design spec
docs/plans/        the phased implementation plans
```

## Quickstart (local, ~2 minutes)

```bash
# 1. start the service (leave running; local, no login)
npx convex dev
#    copy CONVEX_SITE_URL from .env.local  -> this is your $SITE

# 2. create a project -> prints a submit token (public) and admin key (secret)
npx convex run projects:create '{"slug":"myapp"}'

# 3. build the widget and open the demo
npm run build --workspace feedback-sdk-widget
npx http-server -p 8080 .
#    open http://localhost:8080/examples/demo.html, paste $SITE + submit token,
#    click Mount, use the Feedback button.
```

Full walkthrough, including wiring the widget into a real React/Svelte app:
[`docs/TESTING.md`](docs/TESTING.md).

## Using the widget in an app

```bash
npm install feedback-sdk-widget
```

The widget is a browser custom element (`class extends HTMLElement`). **Import it
on the client only** -- importing at module top level crashes any server-rendering
framework (Next.js, SvelteKit, Nuxt) because `HTMLElement` does not exist on the
server. Use the guarded pattern for your stack:

Plain client-side app (Vite/CRA, no SSR):

```js
import "feedback-sdk-widget";
// <feedback-widget endpoint="https://your-service" token="fbk_myapp_..."></feedback-widget>
```

React with SSR / Next.js -- import in an effect:

```jsx
import { useEffect } from "react";
export function Feedback({ endpoint, token }) {
  useEffect(() => { import("feedback-sdk-widget"); }, []);
  return <feedback-widget endpoint={endpoint} token={token} />;
}
```

SvelteKit -- import in `onMount` (browser only):

```svelte
<script>
  import { onMount } from "svelte";
  onMount(() => import("feedback-sdk-widget"));
</script>
<feedback-widget {endpoint} {token}></feedback-widget>
```

Attributes:

- `endpoint` (required) -- your service URL (`CONVEX_SITE_URL`)
- `token` (required) -- the project's public submit token (`fbk_...`)
- optional: `categories` (csv), `page-context`, `label`, `submitter`
- theming: override `--fw-accent`, `--fw-surface`, `--fw-text`, `--fw-radius`, and friends
- fires `feedback-submitted` (`CustomEvent<{ id: string }>`) on success

The panel has an "Attach screenshot" control: the submitter can attach an image
(a screenshot they took) so the agent gets visual context alongside the text.
The image is stored in the service, and each row in the read below carries a
`screenshotUrl` (or `null`) the agent can fetch. Max 3 MB per image.

The public submit token is safe to ship in your app. The admin key is not -- it
stays in your terminal/agent.

## The agent loop

Feedback is read and resolved over HTTP with the admin key. An agent can run
these directly:

```bash
# read the queue (newest first)
curl -s "$SITE/feedback" -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_KEY"

# mark one handled
curl -s -X POST "$SITE/feedback/resolve" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"id":"<feedback id>","status":"done"}'

# delete one (spam / noise)
curl -s -X POST "$SITE/feedback/delete" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"id":"<feedback id>"}'
```

So in practice: submit feedback from the app, then tell your agent "read the
feedback for `myapp` and fix the top item."

## Security model

- Two keys per project: a public **submit token** (write-only, embeddable,
  one project) and a secret **admin key** (read + resolve, terminal-only). Keys
  are stored hashed.
- Every read is scoped to exactly one project server-side -- one project can
  never read another's feedback.
- The submit endpoint sends CORS headers so the browser widget can post
  cross-origin; tokens, not origin, are the security boundary.

## Development

```bash
npm install
npx convex dev --once   # generate the API / deploy locally
npm test                # 31 tests: service, client, widget
```

## Roadmap

- Done: widget published to npm; service deployable to a public cloud endpoint.
- CLI: `npx feedback-sdk init` to provision a project and print keys.
- MCP server so agents get `feedback_list` / `feedback_resolve` tools directly.
- Multi-tenant (accounts, dashboard) to open it beyond a single owner.

## 1. Is the Convex DB "already in feedback-sdk"?

No, and this trips a lot of people up. The `convex/` folder in feedback-sdk is **source code** (schema + functions), not a running database. A Convex "deployment" is a hosted backend instance living on Convex's servers. The source has to be deployed onto one before any data exists or any URL responds.

There's no shared, pre-running feedback DB out there that you point at. The SDK is single-tenant by design - the README says it plainly: "the service runs either as a local Convex deployment or a cloud deployment." **You host your own.** That's why `npx convex dev` is needed once: it turns that source into a live DB + HTTP endpoint that's actually reachable.

## 2. Isn't the npm install enough? Why clone?

The npm package `feedback-sdk-widget` is **only the widget** - the frontend button. That part you already have from npm, no clone needed. Correct instinct.

But the widget is just a form that POSTs somewhere. The **backend** it POSTs to (the `convex/` service - projects, tokens, feedback storage, HTTP routes) is **not published to npm**. It only exists in the GitHub repo. So to run your own backend, you need its source - that's the only reason I cloned it.

And to be clear: I cloned it as a **sibling** directory next to `euno-app`, not inside it. It's not a dependency of your app and doesn't touch your repo. It's a separate little service you deploy once and forget.

## So you have two honest paths

| | **Separate deploy** (current plan) | **Merge into Euno's Convex** |
|---|---|---|
| Clone/second repo | Yes, kept as sibling | No - deleted after |

Here's my honest read, having taken it the whole way - from first line to live in production, including the parts that went sideways.

## The integration process

The actual work was tiny. The friction was all in *understanding the model*, not doing it.

The real integration is 5 files, ~15 meaningful lines: one component, a dependency, two lines in `App.tsx`, two type-declaration files. Once I knew what I was doing, it was a 10-minute job. That's the honest baseline - the SDK's core surface is genuinely small.

But I did not know what I was doing for a while, and that's the first real critique. The README's quickstart walks you straight into "clone the repo, run `npx convex dev`, deploy your own backend." So I cloned it, installed its deps, and started prepping a whole separate Convex deployment. That was wasted work. The truth - one shared hosted service, every app is just install + two env vars - lives in `INTEGRATING.md`, a different doc that nothing pointed me to. A tool's landing doc should not lead with the rarest path (self-hosting your own instance). Most people want "here's a URL and a token, go." That should be the first thing you read, and it wasn't.

Second process note, not the SDK's fault but worth saying: because the widget touches your app's real UI files, the integration collided with everything else moving in the repo (a stale branch 46 commits behind, an `App.tsx` that got rewritten by another feature mid-flight). The SDK didn't cause that, but a feedback widget is inherently a thing that lives in your most-edited file, so expect it to need a rebase if your app is active. The change being *small and isolated* is what made that rebase a 30-second fix instead of a mess - credit to the design there.

## The code itself

This is where it's genuinely good. It's a browser custom element - `class extends HTMLElement`, Shadow DOM, themeable via CSS variables. That means:

- No framework lock-in. No React wrapper to version-match against your React version. It's just an HTML tag.
- Style isolation is real - Shadow DOM means it can't leak CSS into your app or vice versa. I dropped it into a dark constellation-themed app and it didn't fight anything.
- The contract is frozen and documented: `endpoint`, `token`, a few optional attributes, one `feedback-submitted` event. That's a clean, small API surface that won't rot.

The one code-level wart: the published npm package ships its JS bundles with **no `.d.ts`**, even though `package.json` points `types` at a file that isn't in the tarball. Any TypeScript app using the recommended dynamic-import pattern hits `TS7016` and has to hand-write an ambient declaration (I did). That's a straight packaging bug, and it'll bite every single TS consumer until they ship the types. For a TS-first ecosystem, that's the kind of thing that makes an SDK feel unfinished on first contact.

## Developer experience

Middle-of-the-road, dragged up by the code and down by the onboarding.

Good: the `npm install` + drop-a-tag flow is about as low-friction as feedback tools get. The security model is thoughtful - two keys per project, a public write-only submit token (safe to ship in the bundle) and a secret admin key (never leaves your terminal). That's real least-privilege, not theater. CORS is wide open by design with the token as the boundary, which is the correct call for an embeddable widget and saved me any origin-allowlist fiddling.

Rough: the token handoff is manual. There's no self-serve - someone has to mint a project and hand you a `fbk_...` out of band. The roadmap's `npx feedback-sdk init` would close that, but today it's a person-to-person step. And the SSR footgun (importing at module top level crashes any server-render because `HTMLElement` doesn't exist on the server) is real - the docs do call it out, but it's the kind of thing that'll generate confused bug reports from Next.js users who skimmed.

## Agent experience

This is the actual thesis of the SDK - "the inbox is an agent work queue, not a dashboard" - and it's the most interesting part, so I'll be pointed about it.

What works, and works well: I read the queue with a single `curl` and an admin key, got back clean JSON, and could resolve/delete items the same way. No SDK, no auth dance, no pagination ceremony. An agent can operate this with three curl commands it can construct from memory. The JSON shape is sensible and flat. The `screenshotUrl` field is a genuinely smart touch - the submitter can attach what they saw, and the agent gets visual context alongside the text, which is exactly what an agent triaging "this looks broken" actually needs.

Where it's still early: there's no MCP server yet (it's on the roadmap), so the agent has to shell out to curl rather than having first-class `feedback_list` / `feedback_resolve` tools. That's the difference between "an agent can do this" and "an agent reaches for this naturally." Right now it's the former. The moment the MCP server lands, the pitch goes from clever to sticky, because then the feedback queue is just *there* in the agent's toolset, same as reading a file.

The other honest gap: it's single-tenant. One owner, one set of projects, keys handed out manually. Great for dogfooding your own app (which is exactly what we did), not yet a thing you'd hand to a team without the accounts/dashboard layer that's still ahead.

## The verdict

The *idea* is right and slightly ahead of its tooling. "Feedback lands where your agent already works, not in a dashboard a human has to babysit" is a genuinely good reframe, and the bones - custom element, two-key security, curl-able queue, screenshot context - are the correct bones. Nothing about the architecture is wrong.

What holds it back is all fixable and none of it is the core design: ship the TypeScript types, make `INTEGRATING.md` the front door instead of the self-host path, add the provisioning CLI, ship the MCP server. Do those four and this goes from "a clever thing I had to be walked into" to "the obvious way to wire feedback into an agent-built app."

If you're asking whether it was a better process than a typical feedback tool: the *mechanism* yes, clearly - once you're past onboarding, it's less code and a better security model than dropping in something like a hosted form widget. The *onboarding* no - the misleading README cost me real time and would cost any first-timer the same. That gap between "how good it is once you get it" and "how hard it is to get it" is the single most important thing to close.
